name: wireshark
plain: `wireshark` is a graphical program that captures network traffic (or opens a saved .pcap) and shows every packet with its layers decoded. It is the tool to look at a conversation and read it.
Three areas matter: the packet list (one line per packet), the packet details (the protocol layers you can expand) and the bytes (raw hex). Filters at the top bar decide which packets you see.
The command-line twin is tshark. Use Wireshark to explore, tshark to extract in scripts.
when: Follow a TCP or HTTP stream and read it.
Find clear-text passwords, files and DNS names.
Capture live traffic on a lab network.
Decrypt TLS with a key log file.

examples.title: Open a capture
examples.explain: Starts the GUI with the file. Without an argument you pick a file or a network interface.

examples.title: Capture live on an interface
examples.explain: -i picks the interface and -k starts capturing at once.

examples.title: Filter by protocol
examples.explain: Type this in the display filter bar. It shows only HTTP packets. Green bar means the filter is valid.

examples.title: Filter by host and port
examples.explain: Packets to or from this IP and port. && means and, || means or.

examples.title: Find text in packets
examples.explain: Shows packets containing that string anywhere.

examples.title: Follow a stream
examples.cmd: Right-click a packet > Follow > TCP Stream
examples.explain: Rebuilds the whole conversation as readable text. Red is client data, blue is server data. In a CTF this often holds the flag.

examples.title: Export files
examples.explain: Lists files transferred over HTTP (and SMB, TFTP and others) so you can save them.

examples.title: See who talks the most
examples.explain: Tables of address pairs with packets and bytes. Sort by bytes to find the biggest transfer.

examples.title: Decrypt TLS
examples.cmd: Edit > Preferences > Protocols > TLS > (Pre)-Master-Secret log filename
examples.explain: Point it at the key log file from the browser and HTTPS traffic appears decrypted.

mistakes: Mixing the capture filter (stores less) and the display filter (hides).
Reading only the packet list: expand the details to see the real data.
Forgetting that HTTPS needs the key log to be readable.
Capturing on the wrong interface (the VPN is tun0).
Opening untrusted captures on your main machine: dissectors have had bugs; use the lab VM.
